judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long string of 'Whereas' recitals full of aspirational and open-textured language ('regional assets', 'greatest benefits', 'most efficient service in the public welfare') with no operative bite of its own. The vagueness is characteristic of preambles and rarely produces a nameable ambiguous term standing alone.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This is the classic recital-versus-operative-text situation: the preamble's sweeping account of what the 'comprehensive plan administered by a basin wide agency' will do is routinely invoked to expand or contract the operative reach of Sections 1.2(g), 3.8 and 13.1, and courts construing the compact's scope reach for it. That mismatch between broad purposive recital and the narrower operative definitions gives a court something real to construe.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare short-title clause; the only defect is a doubled period after 'Short title..', which changes nothing. No term carries competing meanings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Section 1.2(c) defining 'Compact' as Part I of this act, though 'this Act' versus 'compact' is used loosely across the instrument. Nothing operative turns on it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A definitional preamble whose only soft edge is the escape hatch 'except as may be otherwise required by the context', which by design lets defined terms float. That escape clause is itself a lever an advocate could pull.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It governs every defined term, including the heavily contested 'project' in 1.2(g); the 'unless the context otherwise requires' formula is exactly what a party would cite to escape the definition in Section 3.8. Still, standing alone it creates no conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Area of drainage into the Delaware River and its tributaries' is a hydrologically determinate boundary; 'including Delaware Bay' resolves the one doubtful case. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Coheres with Section 2.7 (commission acts 'within the limits of the basin') and 11.3. No conflicting definition elsewhere.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A pure naming definition tied to Section 2.1. Nothing ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2.1 creates exactly this body; no other provision uses 'commission' differently, save the lower-case references to state water resources commissions in the New York sections, which are contextually clear.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Compact shall mean Part I of this act' is a simple mapping, though 'this act' shifts meaning depending on which of the five enacting statutes is read. That latent referential slippage is minor.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Part II contains five different enacting 'Acts', and Section 15.1 repeatedly distinguishes 'this Act' from 'the Compact'; the definition thus does real work but also sits awkwardly across the five enactments. The tension is theoretical rather than operative.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Net induced adverse effects, whether or not compensated for' is genuinely vague — it has no measurable boundary, and 'commitment' as a species of expenditure is odd. A cost-allocation fight would turn on those words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It feeds Sections 11.4, 13.3 and 15.1(a), which speak of cost allocation and apportionment without cross-referencing the definition; nothing squarely contradicts it. Fit is loose but not incoherent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A sprawling definition ending in the catch-all 'or to facilitate any other uses of any of them', preceded by long enumerated specifics — the paradigm general-versus-specific problem, and 'necessary, useful or convenient' has no boundary. 'Facility' is also embedded in the contested 'project' definition, so its reach matters.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interlocks with 1.2(g) ('any separate facility undertaken... within a specified area') so that the breadth of 'facility' directly drives the scope of Section 3.8 review, and Sections 4.5 and 9.3 then carve back out ('shall not be construed to authorize... distributing water'). Those carve-backs suggest the drafters themselves feared the definition swept too far.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Any appropriate branch, department, bureau or division thereof, as the case may be' is circular — 'appropriate' is undefined and does the work. Mild but nameable vagueness.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1 repeatedly allocates powers among the President, Congress and specific agencies without reference to this definition, but nothing contradicts it. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: This is the definition a federal court had to construe: 'any work, service or activity which is separately planned, financed, or identified by the commission, or any separate facility... for the conservation, utilization, control, development or management of water resources' is grammatically and substantively ambiguous — it is unclear whether 'identified by the commission' modifies all three verbs, whether the purposive clause limits 'work, service or activity' as well as 'facility', and whether a purely private extractive activity qualifies. Two reasonable readings, drastically different in scope, sit on the same words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its reach is only intelligible read against Section 3.8's 'substantial effect on the water resources of the basin', Section 1.5's promise to preserve existing state agencies, Section 3.6(b)'s enumerated standards, and the preamble's list of subjects — and those provisions pull in opposite directions on whether private, non-water-supply activity is a 'project'. Reading the instrument as a whole does not dissolve the tension; it sharpens it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A closed, exhaustive list of four states plus the federal government; no catch-all, no vague term. Clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Because 'signatory party' includes the federal government, Section 12.8's exemption of bonds from 'all taxation by or under authority of any of the signatory parties' collides with Section 15.1(f), which denies federal tax exemption. This definition is the hinge of that conflict, though the defect lies more in 12.8.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Water and related natural resources in, on, under, or above the ground, including related uses of land, which are subject to beneficial use, ownership or control' turns on the undefined and elastic word 'related' — twice — and 'related uses of land' could swallow almost any land use. A court deciding what activities affect 'water resources' must construe this.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the operative measure in Section 3.8 ('substantial effect on the water resources of the basin'), in 3.6(b), and in the Article 11 rules, so its breadth is contested wherever the commission's regulatory reach is contested. Section 14.19's saving of riparian rights and Section 1.5's preservation of state agencies pull the other way.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare introductory phrase to a set of legislative findings; nothing to construe on its own face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It labels what follows as 'find and declare' — findings, not operative commands — which is exactly the recital/operative fault line that matters when 1.3(e)'s purposes are used to expand Section 3.8. The introduction itself contributes little.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A declaratory finding using broad but non-operative language ('affected with a local, state, regional and national interest'). No enumerated list, no catch-all to fight over.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: As a finding it can be marshalled against operative limits like Section 1.5 and 14.19, but standing alone it does not contradict any operative term. Modest.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Declares a purpose of 'joint exercise of such powers of sovereignty'; abstract, but no term whose boundary must be fixed to decide anything.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sits comfortably with Section 1.4 (reserving congressional powers) and 5.5 (reserving state pollution authority), which qualify the 'joint exercise'. No genuine inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A finding that a single administrative agency is 'essential'; rhetorical rather than operative, with no term whose meaning is disputed.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It says a single agency is essential, while Sections 1.5, 5.5, 10.8, 11.1(c) and 11.2(c) all preserve the authority of existing federal and state agencies — a finding that points one way against operative text pointing another. That is a live recital-versus-operative tension a party would exploit.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A factual prediction from 1961 ('ample to meet all presently projected demands'), and a run-on sentence joining two unrelated ideas without punctuation. The mechanical looseness does not change any obligation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The finding that water is 'ample' sits uneasily with Article 10's elaborate machinery for shortage, protected areas and drought emergencies, but that is a difference in register, not an operative conflict. Modest.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A list of purposes ending with the sweeping 'apply the principle of equal and uniform treatment to all water users who are similarly situated' — 'similarly situated' is undefined and would have to be construed if invoked. Otherwise the language is hortatory.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This purposes clause is the standard lever for reading Section 3.8 and the 1.2(g) 'project' definition broadly or narrowly, and it is in tension with Section 1.5's preservation of existing agencies and 14.19's saving of riparian rights. Courts construing the compact's regulatory reach reach for this text.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two saving sentences using conventional formulae ('nothing... shall be construed to relinquish', 'in derogation of'); the scope of 'any navigable waters within the basin' is settled federal usage. Little to fix.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly incorporated by Section 11.1 ('subject in each case to the provisions of Section 1.4'), by 15.1(b)'s proviso and by 15.1(t), which makes the United States' membership contingent on this section's validity — heavy cross-traffic, but all of it deliberate. The relationships are coordinated, not conflicting.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'To the extent not inconsistent with the compact' and 'to the fullest extent it finds feasible and advantageous' are both open-ended, and the section both states a purpose and gives a directive without saying which controls. A party resisting commission jurisdiction would name 'not inconsistent' as the ambiguous hinge.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It promises to preserve existing state and federal offices, which runs against Section 3.8's blanket submission requirement, Section 10.8's supersession of state permits, and Section 1.3(c)'s 'single administrative agency' finding. It is also expressly incorporated by 7.4(b) and 8.2(b), so its meaning propagates.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The renewal window — 'not later than 20 years nor sooner than 25 years prior to the termination' — is expressed in an inverted, counter-intuitive order that invites misreading, and 'none of the signatory states' excludes the federal government without saying so. The window is workable but the drafting is a trap.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coordinates with 1.6(b) and with Section 15.1(q)'s reserved congressional right to repeal, which could end federal participation without triggering this clause. That gap is real but was addressed by 15.1(t).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short wind-up clause that defers wholly to 'act of the Congress'; no term needs construing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It leaves dissolution mechanics to Congress even though the states may terminate under 1.6(a), and it says nothing about bondholders' rights under 12.18 and 12.19. A latent gap, but not a contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Body politic and corporate... as an agency and instrumentality of the governments of the respective signatory parties' is standard compact language, but the dual federal-and-state characterisation is exactly the kind of hybrid status that gets litigated. Still, no single ambiguous term drives an outcome here.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It calls the commission an instrumentality of all signatory parties including the United States, while Section 15.1(m) directs that for FTCA and Tucker Act purposes 'the commission shall not be considered a Federal agency' and 15.1(n) denies federal-employee status to its staff. That is a genuine characterisation conflict a litigant would press.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'One commissioner to be appointed by the President... to serve during the term of office of the President' is a definite term of service; the phrase is clear on its face. No lexical problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The compact's own Endnote states flatly that 'Sections 2.2 and 15.1(d) were inconsistent as to the term of the federal representative's appointment' — a conflict so real that Congress repealed 15.1(d) to fix it, and WRDA 2007 then displaced 2.2 again. This is a named, documented internal contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Detailed and internally consistent: appointment, term, removal at pleasure, and vacancy filling are each addressed. 'Unless otherwise provided by law of the signatory party' is a clean deferral.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(d) made the federal alternate serve at the President's pleasure notwithstanding Article 2, and New York § 631 supplies a further substitute if both member and alternate are absent — layered, but the notwithstanding language sequences them. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Serve without compensation but may be reimbursed for necessary expenses' is a familiar and workable formula; 'necessary' is a common standard courts apply routinely.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(r) provides that 'the provisions of Sections 2.4 and 2.6... notwithstanding', the federal member may be paid compensation by the United States — a direct exception, but one drafted as an express override rather than a conflict. New York § 631(2) adds its own reimbursement source.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'A majority of the membership' is precise (a majority of five, not of those present), and the one-vote rule is flat. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Several provisions require unanimity instead — 3.3(a) emergency action, 3.5(c)-(d) consent of decree parties, and 13.3(b)(2)'s 'unanimous vote' apportionment — but each is an express carve-out from the majority default. Coordinated, not contradictory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Straightforward self-organisation powers with a definite annual officer election; no vague operative term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(r) overrides it as to compensation of the federal member's advisor, and New York § 632 designates the mayor of New York City as its advisor — both are supplements contemplated by the 'in his discretion' language. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Whenever such action may be necessary or convenient to effectuate its powers' is elastic, and the final sentence's 'such power' is ambiguous as to whether the consent requirement covers only the extraterritorial acts or the sale of water too. The referent of 'such power' is a nameable problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be squared with 1.2(e), which defines 'facility' to include property 'within or without the basin', and with 3.6(a)'s unrestricted power to own and operate facilities; the consent-of-the-state condition here is the only brake. That interaction is workable but contested at the edges.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Three mandatory but wholly general sentences ('shall develop and effectuate plans, policies and projects'); the language is aspirational rather than boundary-drawing. Nothing here needs a definition.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It states the commission's mission in terms that Articles 3 through 13 then specify, and it is a natural source for arguing that commission powers are broader than the enumerated ones. But there is no operative provision it contradicts.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare directive to formulate and adopt three documents 'in accordance with Article 13'. Clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Article 13 restates the same three obligations in different words — 13.2 fixes 'six years' where 3.2(b) says only 'such reasonably foreseeable period' — so the two articles duplicate each other imperfectly. The cross-reference here is what makes that duplication visible.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Comprehensive plan... for the immediate and long range development and uses of the water resources' — 'immediate and long range' is loose, but the paragraph is a direction to adopt, not a standard to apply.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It differs from Section 13.1 in consultation requirements (here 'water users and interested public bodies'; 13.1 adds 'public utilities' and requires public hearings), a small mismatch between two statements of the same duty. Nothing irreconcilable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'For such reasonably foreseeable period as the commission may determine' delegates the horizon entirely to the commission, and 'all public and private projects affecting the basin' is very broad without a threshold. The absence of any 'substantial effect' qualifier here is notable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 13.2 covers the same water resources program but fixes 'the ensuing six years or such other reasonably foreseeable period', and Section 3.8's approval trigger is limited to projects of 'substantial effect' while this paragraph sweeps in 'all public and private projects affecting the basin'. That mismatch in threshold is a real handle for argument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A plain requirement of two budgets consistent with the water resources program. Definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 13.3 elaborates the same budgets and adds the apportionment and certification machinery; no inconsistency between them. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'In accordance with the doctrine of equitable apportionment' imports an entire body of contested judicial doctrine as the operative standard, and 'as need appears' is unbounded. Both are nameable open terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The allocation power granted here is immediately hemmed in by 3.3(a)-(c), 3.4 and 3.5, and 3.3(b) says allocations are not 'an apportionment of the waters of the basin among the parties' even though the power is granted 'in accordance with the doctrine of equitable apportionment'. That is close to saying the commission may apportion but its apportionment is not an apportionment.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long single sentence with a proviso that reverses the rule in emergencies; 'impair, diminish or otherwise adversely affect' is a broad catch-all after two specifics, and 'catastrophe' is undefined. The unanimity requirement appears twice with different referents (parties to the decree, then members of the commission), which is easy to conflate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be read with 3.4, 3.5 and New York § 633, which conditions New York's consent on prior approval of its water resources commission; the interlocking consents are intricate but deliberate. The emergency proviso, however, sits in tension with 3.5's flat prohibition on impairing the decree.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The proviso preserving power 'to enter into covenants with respect to water supply' is a sizeable exception carved from a flat prohibition, and 'a benefit or development of the water resources' reads as a drafting slip for 'the benefit'. The relationship between the rule and its proviso is genuinely unclear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It denies that allocations constitute an 'apportionment' while 3.3's opening invokes 'the doctrine of equitable apportionment', and the covenant power it preserves can outlast any particular allocation. That internal pull is the kind courts have to resolve.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Any proper party deeming itself aggrieved' leaves 'proper party' undefined, and the split between de novo Supreme Court review for out-of-basin diversions and ordinary review elsewhere turns on the undefined phrase 'out-of-basin diversion'. Both are nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It creates a second review track alongside 3.8's and 10.6's 'judicial review in any court of competent jurisdiction' and alongside 15.1(p)'s grant of original federal district court jurisdiction, and New York § 634 defines the phrase differently again for different sections. Multiple overlapping review provisions invite argument about which governs.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A dense waiver with two nested exceptions, one of which ('to effectuate rights, powers, duties and obligations under Section 3.3') nearly swallows the waiver, since 3.3 is the very allocation power. The double 'increase or decrease' and the exception's asymmetry (only increases) invite construction.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with 3.3(a) and 3.5, the waiver is qualified by the same emergency and consent machinery, and New York § 633 layers a state-law consent requirement on top. The Section 3.3 exception makes the relationship between the waiver and the allocation power circular.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Nothing in this compact shall be construed in any way to impair, diminish or otherwise adversely affect' is a broad saving clause, and 'To this end, and without limitation thereto' signals the list that follows is illustrative — the classic general-versus-specific setup. But the drafting flags this expressly.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It begins 'Except as specifically provided in Sections 3.3 and 3.4', yet 3.3(a) permits the commission to alter decree diversions in an emergency, so the exception and the prohibition overlap. Also relevant to 14.14(a)'s carve-out for property connected to decree diversions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Impede or interfere with' is broad but familiar; the paragraph is a flat prohibition with no list to construe against. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It flatly bars any action interfering with the decree, while 3.3(a) allows exactly such interference on unanimous emergency consent — the 'Except as specifically provided' opener in 3.5 is the only reconciler. Workable but contested.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Any fee, charge or assessment with respect to diversions... permitted by said decree' is definite and closed. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits alongside 3.7 (rates and charges), 4.3 (assessable improvements), 11.3 (reserved state taxing powers) and 15.1(b), which independently bars charges on pre-existing lawful withdrawals — a stack of overlapping charge prohibitions whose combined boundary is unclear. Moderate.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single long clause listing planning, design, construction, operation and control of projects, structures or facilities — specific enough, but 'used in connection with' withdrawals authorised by the decree is elastic. Nameable but modest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It withdraws jurisdiction over decree-related facilities, which cuts directly against Section 3.8's requirement that every project of substantial effect be submitted and approved; 3.8's own 'subject to the provisions of Sections 3.3 and 3.5' is the reconciling text. Deliberate sequencing.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One short sentence with a single condition. Nothing ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with 3.3(a)'s reference to consulting 'the river master under said decree'. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The commission may:' — a bare stem. Nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The permissive 'may' here contrasts with the mandatory 'shall' of 3.1, 3.9 and 8.3, a distinction that matters where a duty is asserted. Otherwise unremarkable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long verb-string ending in 'determined by the commission to be necessary, convenient or useful for the purposes of this compact' — an entirely self-referential standard, and 'activities and services' is broader than the defined 'project'. The self-judging qualifier is the nameable soft spot.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It grants power over 'projects, facilities, properties, activities and services' whereas 1.2(g) defines 'project' more narrowly, and 15.1(a) forbids the commission from taking any project beyond the planning stage without congressional authorisation. That federal reservation directly qualifies this grant.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All projects and facilities in the basin which affect its water resources, including without limitation thereto' followed by six enumerated examples — the express 'without limitation' disclaims ejusdem generis, but the enumerated items (water treatment plants, trunk mains, flood works) are all conventional water infrastructure, which invites the argument that the general words take colour from them. That is exactly the general-versus-specific dispute.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This standards power reaches projects that merely 'affect' water resources, a lower threshold than Section 3.8's 'substantial effect', and the enumerated list has been used to argue that 'project' in 1.2(g) means water-infrastructure works. The two thresholds and the two lists must be harmonised.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Research and data powers, expressly 'including without limitation thereto' a list of technical topics; permissive and non-regulatory, so little turns on the boundary. Low.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Complements 3.6(e) and 13.1's information gathering; nothing contradicts it. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Publicize such information when and as needed for... other purposes' ends an enumerated list with an open catch-all, though nothing coercive rides on it. Minor.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Overlaps with 6.4's flood warning and posting power and 14.12's reporting power without conflict. Low.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Such special ground water investigations... as may be required to formulate and administer the comprehensive plan' is self-limiting by reference to the plan. Definite enough.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Coheres with 13.1 and 3.6(c); no competing provision. Low.
